job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our history workshop, we examined why the 1857 revolt was not just about the greased cartridges, but a result of deep-seated anger. We looked at how the Doctrine of Lapse was used specifically to annex kingdoms without a natural heir, like Jhansi, rather than taking over any kingdom at will. We also analyzed the social impact of Christian missionaries, who were independent religious groups, not government employees, yet their presence caused widespread fear of forced conversion. Furthermore, we studied the role of the peasants, who were heavily burdened by high taxes and were active participants in the uprising, not neutral observers. Finally, we reviewed the aftermath, where the British Crown took direct control, ending the East India Company's rule to ensure tighter administration. This shift proved that the revolt was a complex movement involving diverse groups, from farmers to displaced rulers, all united by their grievances against British policies. By mapping these events, we saw that the spark in Meerut was merely the final push in a long struggle against colonial exploitation.

items.evidence: We looked at how the Doctrine of Lapse was used specifically to annex kingdoms without a natural heir, like Jhansi, rather than taking over any kingdom at will.
items.q: A ruler dies, but his son is alive to inherit. Under the Doctrine of Lapse, what could Britain do?
options: They had no grounds to annex that kingdom
They could annex any kingdom they wanted
They could annex it, just as in Jhansi
They could annex it if he was unpopular
items.explain: The Doctrine of Lapse applied only to kingdoms without a natural heir, not to any kingdom at will.

wrong.why: thinks Britain could take over any kingdom whenever it wanted
copies the Jhansi example without noticing the missing heir
invents a different reason for annexation

items.evidence: We also analyzed the social impact of Christian missionaries, who were independent religious groups, not government employees, yet their presence caused widespread fear of forced conversion.
items.q: Why did many Indians fear the presence of Christian missionaries?
options: They might force people to change religion
They were British officers who collected the taxes
They were sepoys who refused to fight for Britain
They wanted to annex kingdoms without an heir
items.explain: Missionaries were independent religious groups, but people feared they would force conversion.

wrong.why: mixes missionaries up with the sepoys in the story
mixes missionaries up with the Doctrine of Lapse

items.evidence: Furthermore, we studied the role of the peasants, who were heavily burdened by high taxes and were active participants in the uprising, not neutral observers.
items.q: Peasants took part in the revolt. What does this show about it?
options: Anger at the British went beyond the army
Only the sepoys had complaints against Britain
Farmers joined only because of greased cartridges
Farmers followed their landlords without own grievances
items.explain: Peasants, burdened by high taxes, joined actively, so the anger was not limited to the sepoys.

wrong.why: thinks only sepoys were unhappy and peasants were neutral
thinks cartridges were the only cause
thinks peasants had no grievances of their own

items.evidence: Finally, we reviewed the aftermath, where the British Crown took direct control, ending the East India Company's rule to ensure tighter administration.
items.q: What happened to the East India Company's rule after 1857, and why?
options: It ended, so Britain could control India closely
It lasted until 1947 with no real change
It grew stronger by adding many Indian soldiers
It ended, as the Company chose to retire
items.explain: The Crown took direct control and ended Company rule to administer India more tightly.

wrong.why: thinks Britain raised Indian soldier numbers to prevent revolts
gives a made-up reason for the Company ending
